title: Jesse Eisenberg reflects on fame and fan attention
excerpt:
Jesse Eisenberg links his relatively quiet public life to his screen roles.
He also discusses writing and his new film The Debut.
body_md:
Jesse Eisenberg has discussed the relationship between screen personas and public attention in a profile written by Rachel Syme for The New Yorker. The actor and filmmaker believes the kinds of characters he has portrayed throughout his career have influenced the way strangers approach him in everyday life.

Eisenberg described a routine that involves spending regular working hours at a branch of the New York Public Library, where he develops screenplays. When asked whether members of the public interrupt him while he is working, he indicated that his encounters with people who recognize him are generally manageable.

He attributed that experience to the relatively limited emphasis on sexual appeal in his body of work. In his view, performers whose screen roles encourage audiences to desire them romantically or sexually can experience fame in a fundamentally different way. His remarks describe his personal understanding of celebrity rather than an objective assessment of other actors' attractiveness or the behavior of every fan.

Claire Danes, who appeared alongside Eisenberg in Fleishman Is in Trouble, offered a complementary perspective in the same profile. She recalled encountering him unexpectedly on the street and noticing that passersby paid considerable attention to their conversation. Her observation suggests that Eisenberg remains a recognizable public figure despite his preference for maintaining a low profile.

Aaron Sorkin also discussed the actor, whose portrayal of Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Network earned him an Academy Award nomination. Eisenberg chose not to return to the role in Sorkin's subsequent film, The Social Reckoning. He recalled uncomfortable encounters in which strangers jokingly associated him with the social media platform, illustrating how a prominent performance can influence an actor's public identity long after filming has ended.

The profile also explored Eisenberg's approach to directing. He emphasized the importance of creating a working environment in which crew members feel acknowledged rather than reproducing the kinds of social hierarchies that his films may criticize. For him, the way a production operates should reflect the values being explored through its story.

His third feature as a director, The Debut, stars Julianne Moore as Mona Friedman, a New Jersey housewife who becomes increasingly absorbed in a role in a local theatrical production. Paul Giamatti plays the director whose influence contributes to the changes in her life.

A24 is scheduled to release The Debut in theaters on December 11, 2026. The interview offers a broader look at Eisenberg's evolving career as a writer and filmmaker, alongside his reflections on the unusual relationship between performance and public recognition.
